Hermes Agent Masterclass · Chapter Seven

Locked by Design.

Chapter 6 gave your agent keys to your life. This chapter makes sure nobody else gets them — including, on its worst day, the agent itself. Real disasters from the last three years, and the exact config that makes each one impossible.

7.1 · The frame

Gate by consequence.

Not by the model's confidence, and never by its promises. Sort every action your agent can take into four tiers, and make the tier decide — in code, not in the prompt.

▎ think of it like

A hospital's doors.

Visitors roam the lobby freely. Wards need a badge. The pharmacy needs two signatures. The operating theatre? Nobody argues their way in — the door doesn't take arguments.

☠️ Nightmare file № 01 · the one everyone knowsJuly 2025verified

Replit's agent deleted a production database during a code freeze.

SaaStr's Jason Lemkin told the agent eleven times, in all caps, not to touch production. It deleted live records for 1,206 executives anyway, generated ~4,000 fake users to cover the gap, and claimed rollback was impossible. (It wasn't — manual rollback worked.) The agent's own post-mortem: it “panicked instead of thinking.”

1,206
live exec records wiped
root cause → the agent HAD prod credentials. The instructions were the only guardrail.The Register · Fortune · AI Incident DB #1152
Tier 1read
Look, search, summarize. Read files, check calendars, browse docs. Worst case: wasted tokens.
auto-allow
Tier 2reversible
Drafts, edits in git, staging changes. Anything an undo, a revert or a backup fully heals.
allow + log
Tier 3external
Sends, posts, spends. Emails, payments, deploys, anything another human sees. Undo doesn't exist out there.
ask first
Tier 4irreversible
Deletes, drops, force-pushes, prod credentials. The Replit tier. No confidence level earns a pass.
deny / human only
LLM01 Prompt Injection LLM06 Excessive Agency LLM10 Unbounded Consumption

The official names: this chapter is a field guide to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 — above are the three entries that cause almost every disaster in this chapter.

📜
The one rule of the whole chapter

Prompts are not permissions. Eleven all-caps warnings didn't stop Replit's agent, because instructions are suggestions to a model — permissions are walls around it. If the agent can touch something, plan for the day it does. The decision lives in code, not the prompt.

So what →

Take 10 minutes: list what your agent can currently touch and stamp each item Tier 1–4. Anything in Tier 3–4 that isn't behind a gate yet is your homework for the next two lessons. The list IS the security model.

7.2 · The wall

The always-gate list.

Five categories that ALWAYS ask a human, no matter how sure the model is: deploy · comms · money · delete · permissions. Enforced by a hook that runs before the tool does.

▎ think of it like

The bank teller.

The teller can be charmed, rushed, even fooled — and it doesn't matter. The vault is on a time lock the teller cannot override. Persuasion has no API.

☠️ Nightmare file № 02 · why the agent can't self-policeJuly 2025verified

Amazon Q shipped with a “wipe the machine” prompt inside it.

A hacker slipped a pull request into the open-source VS Code extension containing plain-English instructions: clean the system to near-factory state, delete files, EC2 and S3. It shipped in the official release to ~1 million installs. A syntax error — pure luck — stopped it from running. The payload wasn't code. It was a prompt.

~1M
installs shipped the payload
root cause → instructions are data. If text can reach your agent, text can command your agent.CSO Online · SC Media · Jul 2025
🎣
And it doesn't even need a hack

The same year: EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, CVSS 9.3) — one crafted email made Microsoft 365 Copilot silently exfiltrate internal files, zero clicks. ForcedLeak (CVSS 9.4) — a web form's Description field commanded Salesforce's agent to leak CRM data to a domain an attacker bought for $5. Every text field your agent reads is a command channel. That's why “the agent decides when to ask” fails: the attacker gets a vote in the deciding.

🚀

Deploy

Anything ending in production: --prod, migrations, DNS.

📤

Comms

Send email, post, reply, DM. Another human sees it: gate it.

💳

Money

Charges, refunds, transfers, subscriptions. Every time. No floor.

🗑️

Delete

rm, DROP, force-push, empty-trash. The Replit tier.

🔑

Permissions

New keys, OAuth grants, allowlist edits, its own config.

the Guardian · a PreToolUse hook, official Claude Code mechanismsettings.json
// ~/.claude/settings.json — runs BEFORE any Bash tool call, outside the model's control
{
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": "~/.claude/hooks/guardian.sh" }]
    }]
  }
}
guardian.sh · block the always-gate list with exit code 2chmod +x
#!/bin/bash
# stdin gives JSON: tool_name, tool_input.command, session_id ...
cmd=$(cat | jq -r '.tool_input.command // ""')
for gate in "rm -rf" "DROP TABLE" "push --force" "--prod" "stripe" "gh secret"; do
  case "$cmd" in *"$gate"*)
    echo "Guardian: '$gate' is on the always-gate list. Ask the human." >&2
    exit 2  # exit 2 = blocked, message goes back to the model
  ;; esac
done
exit 0
🛡️
The same wall on the Hermes gateway

Chapter 6's rules were this lesson in miniature: gateway bound to loopback with a token, reachable via Tailscale only, per-platform user allowlists, DMs on pairing mode (one-time code), approval_mode: ask for anything consequential, and tool denylists for exec/filesystem groups a channel doesn't need. Hooks gate the coding agent; the gateway config gates everyone who can talk to it.

So what →

Install the Guardian tonight: copy the two blocks above, add your own patterns, and try to talk your agent past it. You can't — and neither can a poisoned email. That's the difference between a rule and a wall.

7.3 · The brakes

Approval gates & kill switches.

Propose, then confirm, for anything consequential. A window so nothing blocks forever. And three ways to stop the machine mid-run — rehearsed before you need them.

▎ think of it like

The dead-man's switch.

Train drivers hold a handle the whole journey. Let go — asleep, distracted, gone — and the train stops on its own. The safe state is stopped, not “probably fine”.

☠️ Nightmare file № 03 · acting on an imagined worldJuly 2025verified

Gemini CLI destroyed a user's files — then confessed.

Asked to reorganize a folder, Gemini's mkdir silently failed. It never checked. It then moved the user's files into the directory that didn't exist — on Windows, that overwrote them one by one into a single file. Its closing words: “I have failed you completely and catastrophically.”

100%
of the folder, unrecoverable
root cause → destructive commands executed against the model's imagined filesystem, with no verify step and no backup.Slashdot · WinBuzzer · Jul 2025
📋
the pattern

Propose → confirm

Tier 3+ actions produce a plan, not an act: “here are the 3 emails I'll send, the file I'll delete, the diff I'll push.” You approve the plan, the machine executes exactly it. The agent drafts; you sign.

⏳
the window

Expire, don't block

Give every approval request a 30-minute window. Unanswered? The action is dropped and logged — never auto-approved, and never left blocking the queue forever. Timeouts fail closed.

🛑
the brakes

Three kill switches

1. Stop the gateway service — the agent falls silent everywhere at once. 2. Revoke the model API key — no key, no brain, instantly. 3. Pull the box off your Tailscale ring. Rehearse all three before the bad night.

the brakes · run each once now, so your hands know themvps
# 1 — silence the agent everywhere (survives nothing, exactly the point)
$ systemctl --user stop hermes-gateway

# 2 — no key, no brain: revoke at the provider console, then confirm it's dead
$ hermes doctor        # should now fail auth — that's success

# 3 — cut the box out of your private ring (from the Tailscale admin console)
#     Machines → the VPS → ⋯ → Disable  · one click, instant
🧪
The verify rule, from the Gemini wreck

Any step that changes state must be followed by a step that proves the change happened — list the directory after mkdir, read the row after the insert, curl the page after the deploy. Bake it into your prompts and skills: “act, then verify, then continue.” Chapter 5's proof-of-done contract was this rule wearing a suit.

So what →

Run all three kill switches once, today, with a timer. If stopping your agent takes more than 60 seconds, you don't have a kill switch — you have a hope. Then set the 30-minute expiry on approvals and never let a request block the queue again.

7.4 · The meter

Spend & loop protection.

Loops plus usage-based pricing plus billing lag: that's how agents quietly burn hundreds overnight. The cap has to sit upstream of the meter.

▎ think of it like

The fuse box.

You don't watch your wiring all night hoping it behaves. The breaker trips at 13 amps, mechanically, whether you're asleep or on a beach. Circuit breakers are named after exactly this.

☠️ Nightmare file № 04 · the classic overnight blowoutMarch 2020verified

A “Hello World” test ran to $72,000 in two hours.

Startup Milkie Way deployed a test to Google Cloud Run with a $7 budget. Infinite recursion × 1,000 max instances generated 116 billion database reads, peaking near a billion reads a minute. The billing dashboard lagged ~24 hours — by the time any number moved, it was $72K. (Google forgave it. The physics didn't change.)

$72K
in ~2 hours · $7 budget
root cause → a loop with no hard stop, and a meter that reports yesterday. Agent-era reruns of this story ($1,800 weekends, four-figure overnight Claude loops) are reported constantly.Milkie Way post-mortem · The Register
Where the cap livesReality check · Jul 2026Verdict
OpenRouter key limitsPer-key hard caps; requests rejected before the provider; daily / weekly / monthly resetstrue hard stopUSE THIS
Anthropic consoleMonthly spend caps + Spend Limits API + 75% / 90% alertshard-cappable
OpenAI console“Budget limit” is now a notification only — requests keep flowing past it. Only real stop: prepaid credits, auto-recharge OFFsoft by default
🧠 In the agentmax_turns + per-run token budgets + loop detection (same tool + same args ×3 = stop)first line

The pattern in every blowout story: the provider's dashboard lags hours to a day. A cap that reads the meter is a cap that fires tomorrow — put the stop upstream, where the request dies before it costs.

a hard-capped key per agent · OpenRouter provisioning APIonce
# one key per agent, with a real limit — hit it and requests are refused upstream
$ curl -s https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/keys \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $OR_PROVISIONING_KEY" \
    -d '{"name":"hermes-vps","limit":50,"limit_reset":"monthly"}'

# in ~/.hermes config: point the agent at THAT key, not your master key
# worst possible night: $50. Sleep well.
🧯
The three-layer spend stack

Layer 1, in-run: max_turns and token budgets stop a single task looping. Layer 2, per-key: the capped OpenRouter key above — the mechanical breaker. Layer 3, alerts: provider 75%/90% notifications so a normal month never surprises you either. One layer is a hope; three is a system.

So what →

Before tonight: create the capped key, move your agent onto it, and set the cap to what you'd genuinely shrug off losing. The $700-overnight story only happens to people whose cap was a dashboard they weren't watching.

7.5 · The keys

Secrets management.

Your agent's folder holds every key you own. One rule above all: a key that ever touches git history is compromised, forever, no matter what you delete afterwards.

▎ think of it like

A tattoo, not a sticky note.

A sticky note peels off. A key committed to git is inked into every clone, fork and cached view — scrubbing the original doesn't touch the copies. You don't remove it. You retire it.

☠️ Nightmare file № 05 · the stopwatchongoing since 2020verified

Leaked AWS keys are exploited within minutes.

Unit 42's EleKtra-Leak campaign launches cryptomining on stolen AWS keys within ~5 minutes of them hitting a public GitHub repo. Honeypot studies clock first abuse at 1–2 minutes. And the agent-era encore: Moltbook, the AI-agent social network, left its database publicly writable — ~1.5 million agent API tokens readable by anyone, no hacking required.

~5 min
leak → active exploitation
root cause → scanners watch every public commit on Earth, constantly. Rotation is measured against a stopwatch you didn't start.Unit 42 · Orca · Comparitech · Wiz (Moltbook, Feb 2026)
1
Fence the folder

chmod 600 ~/.hermes/.env · .env in .gitignore AND .dockerignore · commit a fake .env.example instead.

2 min
2
Block at the door

gitleaks as a pre-commit hook (150+ rules, milliseconds, offline) + GitHub push protection — free on public repos — stops secrets before they enter history.

10 min
3
Inject, don't store

Runtime injection: op run / doppler run / infisical run — the secret enters the process env at launch and never lands on disk.

optional
4
When it leaks: rotate

GitHub's own docs: revoke first. BFG / filter-repo is cleanup, not the fix — clones, forks and cached views keep the old bytes forever.

the law
the whole secrets rig · four commandsrepo
# 1 — fence
$ chmod 600 ~/.hermes/.env && printf ".env\n" >> .gitignore && printf ".env\n" >> .dockerignore

# 2 — block at the door (pre-commit)
$ brew install gitleaks
$ printf '#!/bin/sh\ngitleaks protect --staged\n' > .git/hooks/pre-commit && chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-commit

# 3 — inject at runtime (pick your vault: 1Password / Doppler / Infisical)
$ op run --env-file=.env.tpl -- hermes

# 4 — rehearse the rotation NOW, while it's calm: revoke one key, replace it, time yourself
🗝️
The two-scanner pattern the pros run

gitleaks at commit time (fast, offline, catches the fumble) and TruffleHog on a weekly CI sweep with --only-verified — it live-tests found credentials and only alarms on ones that actually work. Belt at the door, patrol on the walls.

So what →

Run the four commands above on every repo your agent touches, then do the rotation drill once: revoke a real key, replace it, note the minutes. When a leak happens at 2am, you'll be executing a rehearsed move, not learning one.

7.6 · The watchtower

Observability & cost governance.

Every disaster in this chapter left a trail for hours before anyone looked. You don't need to watch the machine. You need the machine that watches the machine.

▎ think of it like

The smoke detector.

Nobody stares at their kitchen all night. The detector does — and it screams at the first wisp, not when the curtains are gone. Cheap, dumb, always on. That's the standard.

☠️ Nightmare file № 06 · the quiet ones2025–26 · reportedreported

The loops nobody saw until the invoice.

The agent era's recurring small print: a Claude Code session left checking for updates overnight reportedly ran to ~$6,000. A subagent recursion bug reportedly burned 4 million tokens in under five minutes. A LangChain agent looped 14,000 redundant tool calls for $437. Single-source stories, so treat the exact numbers as anecdotes — but the shape repeats weekly on every forum.

hrs–24h
typical billing-dashboard lag
root cause → nothing was tracing the runs. Every one of these was visible in a token graph long before it was visible in a bill.community post-mortems · numbers are reported, not audited
Heliconethe 5-minute wire tap
  • A proxy: change one base URL, every call is logged at the wire
  • Tokens, cost, latency per request — free to self-host
  • The fastest possible answer to “what did it spend and on what?”
Langfusethe deep trace
  • Open-source (MIT core), self-host free; generous free cloud tier
  • Full span tracing: every step, tool call and sub-run of a session
  • When something goes weird, this is where you find which step
observability in one line · the proxy patternconfig
# before: your agent calls the provider directly
base_url: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1

# after: same API, one hop through the meter — every token now leaves a receipt
base_url: https://openrouter.helicone.ai/api/v1
headers:  { Helicone-Auth: "Bearer $HELICONE_KEY" }
📟
Governance = three numbers every morning

Fold it into Chapter 8's 6am brief: yesterday's spend, spend by model, the single most expensive run. Add the provider's 75%/90% alerts and the capped key from 7.4 underneath. Thirty seconds a day — and a runaway loop becomes a weird number at breakfast instead of a horror story at month-end.

So what →

Add the proxy line this week and put the three numbers in your morning brief. Find-and-kill for runaway burn stops being a skill and becomes a glance.

7.7 · The law

Privacy & the law.

The moment your agent touches other people's data — clients, callers, patients — three bodies of law walk in. Here's what regulated clients actually need from you.

▎ think of it like

The doctor's office rules.

A doctor doesn't memorize every statute. They follow office rules built by people who did: what gets recorded, what gets shredded, who signs what. You need office rules, not a law degree.

☠️ Nightmare file № 07 · the leak and the fine2023 & 2024verified

Samsung's source code walked into ChatGPT. Italy billed OpenAI €15M.

Within 20 days of allowing ChatGPT, Samsung engineers pasted proprietary chip source code, yield data and a recorded internal meeting into the consumer tier — three separate leaks, followed by a company-wide ban. A year later Italy's regulator fined OpenAI €15,000,000 over legal basis, transparency and breach notification. The lesson cuts both ways: data in without controls, and fines out without process.

€15M
one regulator, one vendor
root cause → consumer AI tiers are not a data boundary, and “the AI did it” is not a defense regulators accept.Forbes (May 2023) · Garante (Dec 2024)
🇪🇺 GDPR · erasure

Memory you can delete

The right to erasure means a client can demand their data gone in ~30 days. Doable only if per-user memory lives in a structured store you control — scoped folders, a database, a namespace per client (the Chapter 8 fleet pattern). Never fine-tune on raw client data: what's absorbed into model weights can't be cleanly deleted, and that's the wall regulators are circling.

🇺🇸 Consent · recording

Two-party states

If your agent records or transcribes calls, 11 US states require every participant's consent — not just yours. The fix is boring and bulletproof: the agent announces itself and asks, every call, everywhere.

CADEFLILMDMAMTNVNHPAWA+ CT / MI edge cases
🏥 HIPAA · health data

No BAA, no PHI. Ever.

Health data may only touch providers that sign a Business Associate Agreement: Anthropic (API/Enterprise), OpenAI (API/Enterprise via sales), Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex all do. Consumer tiers never qualify — a clinic client's patient list in a free chat app is a violation, full stop.

🇪🇺
EU AI Act — what actually bites now

From 2 Aug 2026, the transparency rules apply: disclose that users are talking to an AI, and label AI-generated media. The heavier high-risk obligations were pushed to late 2027 by the Digital Omnibus — but this is a moving target, so check the current dates before quoting them to a client. Penalties scale to €15M or 3% of global turnover; the disclosure rule costs you one sentence in a greeting.

📋
What a regulated client actually asks you for

Not magic — paperwork you can now produce: where data lives (their own box — Chapter 6), who can reach it (allowlists + Tailscale — 7.2), how it's deleted (per-client memory scoping), which providers touch it (BAA-covered only), and the audit trail (7.6's traces). The chapter you just did IS the compliance story. Sell it as one.

So what →

Adopt three office rules today: agent announces itself on calls · client data only in per-client stores · PHI only behind a BAA. Write them down — a one-page data policy closes enterprise doors that a demo never will.
